newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: War crimes prosecutor expects more Bosnia arrests.
newsitem.headline: War crimes prosecutor expects more Bosnia arrests.

text.p: U.N war crimes prosecutor Richard Goldstone said on Wednesday the Bosnian elections should speed up the process of bringing indicted war criminals to justice, including Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic.

"To be optimistic would be overstating it, but I think there are good prospects of an arrest taking place," Goldstone said, referring to Karadzic, the wartime Bosnian Serb leader, and Mladic, his military commander.

Speaking to journalists in The Hague, Goldstone urged the international community to pressure Bosnia's new collective presidency to arrest indicted war criminals in line with the Dayton peace agreement.
"Now is the time to push the newly constituted authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina to carry out their obligations," he said.

"The wheel is turning in the right direction. If the new government...fails to live up to its international obligations it will come into a collision certainly with the European Union, certainly with the Security Council.
"So there are realpolitik reasons to be cautiously optimistic further arrests will take place."
Following Saturday's elections, he said, Bosnia's own police force was now in a position to arrest "expendable ex-politicians" who had been indicted.

Goldstone, a South African judge who hands over his post to Canadian judge Louise Arbour in two weeks, said the one disappointment of his two years as chief prosecutor of the U.N. Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal was the small number of arrests made.
"The credibility and whole future of the tribunal is very much at risk at the moment and the next months are going to be vital in that respect," he said.
Goldstone has repeatedly criticised NATO for failing to capture suspected war criminals, citing it as a major stumbling block to the success of the tribunal.

The tribunal, created by the Security Council in May 1993, has indicted 75 suspects so far but holds only seven of them in its 24-cell detention centre. The first trial began in May and is expected to run for several more weeks.
Goldstone said the tribunal was continuing to investigate suspected war criminals in former Yugoslavia and more indictments would be issued this year and next.
He declined to comment on whether Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic or Croatian President Franjo Tudjman were among those being investigated.
Goldstone said he would rejoin South Africa's constitutional court with "absolutely no bitterness...and a fair sense of achievement".
He said the establishment of the tribunal had sent out a clear message that the world would not tolerate serious violations of international humanitarian law.
"If Karadzic had not been indicted, I don't believe we would have had an election on Saturday," he added.
